comments.text: ITEMNAMES: the addresses of the 256 words items are named with, low bytes here and high bytes at $7000. An item carries three word numbers ($6D7D-$6D7F in the item in hand) and print_item_name ($399B) prints them in turn, so "LONG SWORD +1" is three words. Words 0, 62, 63 and 168 have no text (address 0).
The high bytes of the 256 item words' addresses (item_word_lo, $6F00).

DUNGEON2: unpacks packed data into memory from A (low) and X (high), with all 64 KB RAM showing (all_ram) so it can write under the I/O area. The data's address is taken off the stack, high byte first, so the caller pushes it (low, then high) and jumps here; the RTS at the end goes back to the caller's caller. A byte $00-$7F is copied as it is; $80+n copies the next byte n times; $FF ends. The adventure module's install_wall_def jumps here from $14BC with the wall colours' address.
Copies the byte at the data pointer ($4C/$4D) to the destination ($A7/$A8) and steps the destination on.
Steps the data pointer ($4C/$4D) on by one.

When the two bytes at $C04B, in GDRIVE, equal those at $2B4F in the adventure module, copies $FB/$FC to $2B75/$2B76: the AREA map's square is the party's own, and its screen place is noted (draw_area_map calls it from $12EF).

Adds one to the 16-bit count at $49EC/$49ED in the saved game when X is 4, the days figure of the clock: a count of days. The adventure module's add_time_unit calls it ($0DEF) for every figure it moves.
For each filled party slot whose character has bit 7 of $6BB8 set, clears its fourteen bytes of money ($6BBB-$6BC8) and stores it back. The adventure module's start calls it ($0817).

SEARCH, the Adventure Menu's sixth command: flips the Search flag (bit 0 of $6DCA) and copies it to $6DDE, the copy the module keeps. The adventure module reaches it through its menu_handlers table ($08BC, $08C3).

Prints string X of the adventure module's table (low bytes $0CAD, high $0CD5) at the start of the next row; $7AA3 at the start of row A, $7AAC at the cursor. The adventure module calls it ($0E93, $2522).
print_line's string X at the start of row A.
print_line's string X at the cursor: points $07/$08 at it from the adventure module's table and prints it.

COMBAT3, which INIT loads: the battle's tables. This one turns the joystick's four bits (each 0 while pressed) into a direction, 0 north to 7 north-west, $80 for none or an impossible pair: 14 up 0, 6 up and right 1, 7 right 2, 5 down and right 3, 13 down 4, 9 down and left 5, 11 left 6, 10 up and left 7.
What a step costs in half squares by direction: 2 straight, 3 diagonal. Direction 7's cost is the next table's first byte, 3.
For each undead type 1 to 12 the lowest turning level ($6BA4) that can turn it at all, needing a 20 (turn_roll); type 0 is not undead, and its byte is step_cost's last.
For each undead type the turning level from which turn_number applies.

For each undead type the number a turning roll needs at turn_level, 3 less for each level above: 10 for type 1, 13 for type 2, 16, 19, 19, 19, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16 and 19 for type 12. Below 0 the undead is turned or destroyed whatever the roll. The last byte, 19, would be type 13's.

ITEMS: 128 item types of 16 bytes, read into $6D8C by load_item_type ($363D). Byte 0 is the class the code tests (0 weapon, 1 shield, 2 armour, 9 the ring class two can be readied of, others below 10 one at a time), 1 the hands it takes, 2-4 its damage against large creatures as dice, sides and bonus, 6 bit 7 for a protective item and in its low bits the armour class it gives on the 60-minus scale ($B4, 52, is leather's AC 8; $81 the shield's 1), 9-11 its damage against small and man-sized ones, 13 the classes that may ready it (compared with $6BEB), 14 flags (bit 3 checked by find_readied). Bytes 5 and 12 are set only for weapons that can be thrown or shot (DART 6 and 6, the bows 4 and 16 to 22); find_readied keeps byte 12 of the readied weapon in $6D9C. Types 0-63: 1-47 the weapons in the order of their names (BATTLE AXE 1d8, BARDICHE 2d4/3d4, MORNING STAR 2d4/1d6+1 ... the bows and SLING), 50-58 the armours LEATHER to PLATE, 59 SHIELD.
Item types 64-127 (item_types, $7B00): 64-84 with a class byte and no combat figures, 85-96 with a weapon's, 97-126 all zero, and 127 a weapon's again, 2d20 against both sizes.
Item types 80-127 continued past $8000 (item_types_2, $7F00): the rows of 16 bytes go on in the same layout to type 127 at $82F0.

SOUNDFX's entry for each interrupt, called by irq ($3BEA): $BA03 starts sound A. Plays nothing while a sound is being started ($BD79) or with the volume ($BA06, written to $D418) at 0; otherwise brings in its zero page and steps the three streams (sound_voice, $BA33), then puts its zero page away.
sound_start's jump: the modules start a sound with A, the sound's number (0 silences them all).
The SID volume the driver writes to $D418 each interrupt (0 stops it playing).
The volume sound_start copies to $BA06 when it starts a sound.

The driver's copy of its zero page, $B2-$B9: the three streams' read pointers ($B2/$B3, $B4/$B5, $B6/$B7) and the sound data's base ($B8/$B9, $BD7B). sound_zp_in ($BC59) and sound_zp_out ($BC64) swap them with the zero page.
The body of sound_play, for each interrupt.

Steps stream X and the SID voice of the same number (0, 2 or 4): nothing when the stream's wait ($BD35) and the voice's gate time ($BD42) are both over. Adds the voice's frequency slide ($BD65) to its frequency ($BD53) and its pulse sweep ($BD6B) to its pulse width ($BD59), counts the gate time down and clears the gate bit when it reaches the release point ($BD48), counts the stream's wait down and at 0 reads the stream's next commands (sound_commands). Then writes the voice's frequency, pulse width, envelope and control to its SID registers ($D400 + the offset at $BC78).

Reads a stream's commands until one makes it wait. A byte $00-$0F sets field n under the stream's number (its offset in $BC7D) to the next byte, or the next two from field 10 on, and $00, the wait, ends the step. $40+n is a repeat: two bytes, high first, give a target from the data's base, and the counter n bytes on from the stream's wait is counted down: the stream jumps back while it is not yet 0, and a counter at 0 jumps always. $80+ is a note (sound_note, $BB0E): bits 3-6 pick its length from a list in the data, bits 0-2 its instrument, the next byte its pitch ($3F a rest, bit 7 another note at once). The note takes a free voice, one whose gate time and the wait of the stream of its number are both 0, or the stream's own voice when none is free, and loads the instrument's nine bytes from $BD7B into it unless that voice holds the instrument already.

Starts a note for stream X: its length from the data at $BD7B plus the stream's length base ($BD36), its instrument (bits 0-2, plus one), and a SID voice for it ($BD7A): from the third voice down, the first free one (its gate time, $BD42, and the wait of the stream of its number both 0) that already holds the instrument ($BD4E), or else the lowest free one, or the stream's own voice when none is free. The instrument's control, transposition, release point, envelope and pulse are loaded into that voice unless it holds the instrument already, the frequency set from the note table ($BC8D, pitch plus transposition), the voice's gate time set to the note's length and the gate opened. A pitch byte with bit 7 starts another note in the same step. None of SOUNDFX's twelve sounds has a note: they set the fields directly.
Reads the next byte of stream X into A and $BD77 and steps its pointer ($B2,X) on.

Starts sound A: sets the volume ($BA07 to $BA06), takes the sound's entry from the table at the data's base (six bytes each: the three streams' offsets, 0 for an unused stream) and for each stream used points it there, clears all the stream's fields and gives it a wait of 2. $BD79 keeps sound_play out while it works.
Copies the driver's saved zero page ($BA08) into $B2-$B9.
Copies $B2-$B9 back to the driver's save ($BA08).
Where each of the eight instruments starts in the data at $BD7B: nine bytes apart, 0 to 63.
Each voice's first SID register, by number 0, 2 or 4: $D400, $D407, $D40E.

For each of the sixteen fields a command can set, its offset from the wait ($BD35): 0 the wait, 1 the length base, 6 and 7 and 12 the repeat counters, 13 the gate time, 18 the control, 19 the release point, 24 the transposition, 25 the instrument, then the two-byte ones: 30 frequency, 36 pulse width, 42 envelope, 48 frequency slide, 54 pulse sweep, 60 pulse width to start each note with.
84 SID frequencies, low byte first, seven octaves of semitones from 536 (about 32 Hz) to 64814, read by sound_note.
The high bytes of the note frequencies, every other byte from here (note_frequencies, $BC8D).

The fields, eleven rows of six bytes with a pair for each number 0, 2 and 4 (the row and offset in field_offsets, $BC7D): waits and length bases, repeat counters, gate times, control and release points, transposition and instrument, frequency, pulse width, envelope, frequency slide, pulse sweep, starting pulse width. The wait, length base and repeat counters are a stream's; the rest are the SID voice's of that number, which a note writes into whichever voice it takes and a stream's own commands write under the stream's number.
Each stream's length base, the offset in the data at $BD7B where its list of note lengths starts (the wait's partner in the first row of sound_fields).
Each voice's gate time: a note sets it to the note's length in the voice it takes (sound_note), and sound_voice counts it down; the voice's gate closes when it reaches the release point ($BD48).
Each stream's control: the SID waveform and gate bits written to the voice's control register.
Each voice's release point, the gate time at which sound_voice closes the gate.
Each stream's transposition, added to a note's pitch.
The instrument each voice holds, so a note on the same instrument does not load it again.
Each stream's frequency, low byte; its high byte is at $BD54.
Each stream's pulse width, low byte; its high byte is at $BD5A.
Each stream's pulse width, high byte.
Each stream's attack and decay, written to the voice's $D405.
Each stream's sustain and release, written to the voice's $D406.
Each stream's frequency slide, low byte, added to the frequency each step.
Each stream's frequency slide, high byte.
Each stream's pulse sweep, low byte, added to the pulse width each step.
Each stream's pulse sweep, high byte.
The pulse width a stream's notes start with, low byte.
The pulse width a stream's notes start with, high byte.
The last byte read from a stream (sound_byte).
A working number: the instrument, a counter's number, or six times the sound's number.
Set while sound_start works, so that sound_play leaves the streams alone.
The SID voice a note takes (sound_note).

The twelve sounds, six bytes each: the offsets from here of their three streams, 0 for none. 0 is silence; 1 three sawtooth voices warbling at three pitches; 2 a rising noise burst; 3 a rising pulse tone on three voices five steps apart; 4 a sawtooth trill with a falling end over a slow noise; 5 a high pulse warble; 6 a falling noise on three voices a step apart; 7 a sawtooth warble on two; 8 a high hiss; 9 a low rumble; 10 a short burst then a long rumble; 11 a three-note pulse chord. Frequencies below are the SID's register values, and a step is one call of sound_play.
An instrument's second byte, its transposition, read by sound_note; in SOUNDFX these bytes are the start of sound_table, which no note reads.
An instrument's third byte, its release point.
An instrument's fourth byte, its attack and decay.
An instrument's fifth byte, its sustain and release.
An instrument's sixth byte, the low byte of its starting pulse width.
An instrument's seventh byte, the high byte of its starting pulse width.
An instrument's eighth byte, the low byte of its pulse sweep.
An instrument's ninth byte, the high byte of its pulse sweep; from here on in SOUNDFX the bytes are the rest of sound_table and the sounds' streams.
Sound 10: noise at 1200 for 7 steps, then noise from 300 rising one step at a time for 100, then silence.
Sound 8: noise at 60000 for 20 steps, a hiss.
Sound 9: noise at 1200 for 30 steps, a rumble.
Sound 7, its second stream: one step's wait, then the first stream's warble (sound_7a).
Sound 7: a sawtooth from 1200 swung up and down 30 times by a slide of 200 and back.
Sound 6, its streams two and three: one or two steps' wait before the first stream's noise (sound_6a), so three voices sound it a step apart.
Sound 6: noise from 2000 falling by 50 a step for 10 steps.
Sound 5: a pulse tone at 47000 swung up and down 12 times by 700.
Sound 3, its streams two and three: five and ten steps' wait before the first stream's tone (sound_3a).
Sound 3: a pulse tone at 3000, its pulse width sweeping, rising by 600 a step for 50 steps.
Sound 4, first stream: a sawtooth from 400 rising slowly for 20 steps, a trill of 22 swings, then falling for 30.
Sound 4, second stream: noise from 220 rising slowly for 50 steps and falling for 50.
Sound 2: noise from 10000 rising by 240 a step for 30 steps.
Sound 0, all three streams: the gate closed and the stream ended, silencing the voice.
Sound 1: three sawtooth tones at 4080, 8200 and 7000 (with $BEDB and $BEF8), each swung up and down 6, 10 and 8 times.
Sound 1, second stream: a sawtooth at 8200 swung up and down 10 times.
Sound 1, third stream: a sawtooth at 7000 swung up and down 8 times.
Sound 11: a pulse tone at 3380 for 12 steps, with $BF2A at 8200 and $BF3F at 1500, a chord.
Sound 11, second stream: a pulse tone at 8200 for 12 steps.
Sound 11, third stream: a pulse tone at 1500 for 12 steps.
